element: Scope set by one real or imagined "why" question
what_it_does: It tells the reader the one question the post answers and what it will not cover, so every later sentence can be checked against that question.
when_to_use: At the top of the post, because the draft currently opens with the series goal and ends with optimisation methods, and one stated question tells the reader which of those topics this post is about.

candidates.sentence: This post answers one question: how far does one legal edit move a Pokemon team's win rate, and is that further than one step moves a standard optimisation benchmark? It does not cover which search methods cope with that, such as MAP-Elites, which keeps the best team in each cell of a grid of team traits, or the cross-entropy method, which refits a sampling distribution to its best samples.

facts.claim: The edit is one legal change: a move, an item or a whole Pokemon.
facts.source: notes/research_notes/Landscape analysis inside CEM 20261020/one-edit-evidence.md, section 'September 28 study: different legal edit operators'

facts.claim: The figure compares Pokemon edits with steps on the Pest Control and Hartmann-6 benchmarks.

candidates.sentence: This post answers one question: why should a team that wins become a different team after one changed move? It leaves out the benchmark comparison and the search methods, and stays with what one edit does to one team's win rate.

facts.claim: The rerun gave each of 40 starting teams 18 legal edits of six kinds and replayed each unchanged team three times, with every score taken over 384 battles against the 50 top-placing teams under one behaviour-cloning policy.
The figure does not establish mathematical non-smoothness.

candidates.sentence: This post answers one question: why is Pokemon team building worth studying as a scientific problem? It gives one reason, that one edit can move win rate by more than battle noise, and leaves the other reasons for later posts in the series.

facts.claim: Each per-edit change is compared with the change from an unchanged-team repeat, which shows battle noise.
facts.source: notes/Blog/visuals/smoothness/README.md, section 'Three connected views', Try one edit
